status: First four halls reviewed; Collective Knowledge next
summary: Post-Crisis moves from making distinctions visible, to arranging participation, preserving disagreement and locating a claim. The word study, furniture plans, merge sculpture and four situated readouts offer comparisons the visitor can control. The manuscripts preserve their strongest questions and keep evidence distinct from the authority a display can suggest.

items.title: The words remain; their room changes
items.description: The old physical handle reached only 0.14 of the intended 0–1 blend at full travel. The corrected callback uses its normalized value. COMPRESSION now reaches both arrangements, with no simultaneous brightening or fading of the groups.
captions: Arrangement A: the two authored groups occupy the central region.
Arrangement B: warm positions contract while grey positions spread. Colours, emission and alpha are held fixed.
items.image_note: Same camera, two states of the revised Godot museum. These are not before/after software screenshots. The frozen old callback was executed separately to reproduce the 0.14 endpoint. Tracked hand use remains to be checked.
items.text_kind: book — a preserved question gains a working encounter
items.before: Choose two warm-coloured labels and keep both in view while moving PERSPECTIVE. Compare their changing separation with two grey labels. Stop partway through the movement and notice which words are still easy to distinguish individually.
items.after: Choose two warm-coloured labels and keep both in view while moving COMPRESSION. Compare their changing separation with two grey labels. Stop partway through the movement and notice which words are still easy to distinguish individually. Keep the handle still and move your head. What changes now?

items.title: Move the handle. Then move yourself.
items.description: The text keeps its distinction between an authored analogy and evidence about a trained model. The visitor can now hold the handle still and change viewpoint, separating movement of the representation from movement of the observer.
captions: A, from the controls: the chosen warm labels can be followed individually.
B, from the same position: the warm labels crowd together. The grey labels move farther away.
items.image_note: Actual close views. Fixed materials do not imply identical perceived visibility: distance, overlap and viewing angle are part of this encounter. The 24 terms and their two groupings remain authored choices.
items.text_kind: book — a preserved question gains a working encounter
items.before: The warm group compresses into a smaller region while the grey group spreads and moves away. The words themselves remain, but the space available to tell them apart changes. Presence in a representation is therefore different from being represented with useful distinctions.
items.after: The warm group compresses into a smaller region while the grey group spreads and moves away. The words themselves remain. Their colours and brightness stay fixed while the space available to tell them apart changes. Presence in a representation is therefore different from being represented with useful distinctions.

items.title: The grouping is also something to question
items.description: READ opens the maker’s interpretation without changing the geometry. Its wording asks which distinction matters to the visitor. The study stands on a narrow support with controls around 1.1 m, and the lower divider opening gives the expanded arrangement room. The three secondary works keep their exact placements.
captions: Halfway between A and B, with READ open: “Both groups were chosen.”
The study in the divided gallery, with room to circulate around its expanded state.
items.image_note: 28 interaction/state checks and seven selected walking segments pass in the actual museum copy. The test triggers the real arrival-gate signal before walking; it does not test palm recognition or continuous headset play. All four authored artifact families instantiate.
items.text_kind: book — a preserved question gains a working encounter
items.before: Now scrutinise the groups chosen for the sculpture. Words such as “queer”, “disabled” and “refugee” do not name interchangeable experiences. Nor are “normal”, “professional” and “objective” equivalent claims. The exhibit risks repeating a flattening if its two colours become a sufficient account of everyone they contain.
items.after: Press READ when you are ready to consider the grouping. Both groups were chosen. Now scrutinise the groups chosen for the sculpture. Words such as “queer”, “disabled” and “refugee” do not name interchangeable experiences. Nor are “normal”, “professional” and “objective” equivalent claims. The exhibit risks repeating a flattening if its two colours become a sufficient account of everyone they contain.

items.title: Before the first person speaks
items.description: Applied Ethics begins with one neutral model. The existing HEAD and CIRCLE configurations are now available at the controls; PAIR brings them together. Chair count and relative scale differ, so the text does not pretend this changes arrangement alone.
captions: HEAD: seven chair blocks, including a larger head position.
CIRCLE: six equal chair blocks. These solo models are larger than their paired versions.
items.image_note: Actual states of the revised Godot museum, from the same elevated inspection camera. These are miniature models, not rooms the player can occupy; headset visibility remains to be checked.
items.text_kind: book — existing questions become selectable encounters
items.before: Walk around the two miniature rooms. In the long-table plan, locate the head chair and compare its size with the other chairs. In the circular plan, choose one seat and imagine speaking from it. Trace the distances to the other positions rather than simply choosing the greener model.
items.after:
Begin with HEAD. One miniature room waits on the pedestal. Before anyone speaks, where does your eye place the speaker? Walk around the model and compare the large chair at the end with the smaller ones beside the table.

Press CIRCLE. Choose one position and imagine speaking from it. Trace the distances to the others. Then press PAIR to see both plans together. The models become smaller so they fit beside each other; the panel stays where your hand left it.

items.title: Does the room seem to have made up its mind?
items.description: The existing critique of red authority and green distribution can now be tried. COLOUR and NEUTRAL change furniture materials while every chair keeps its position, orientation and scale.
captions: PAIR, NEUTRAL: both plans in the same furniture colour.
PAIR, COLOUR: the earlier red, tan and green judgements return. No chair moves.
items.image_note: Same camera and geometry. The runtime probe checks every chair transform across this colour change. The passage about equal spacing versus equal opportunity remains unchanged.
items.text_kind: book — existing questions become selectable encounters
items.before: Notice how the exhibit colours its own argument. Red singles out authority; green recommends the distributed arrangement. That visual judgement arrives before you have tested whether the plan meets a particular group’s needs. Looking critically at a model includes looking at the persuasion built into its presentation.
items.after: Leave PAIR in place and press COLOUR. No chair moves. Red now singles out authority; green recommends the distributed arrangement. Does the room seem to have made up its mind? Press NEUTRAL again and see what remains of that judgement. Looking critically at a model includes looking at the persuasion built into its presentation.

items.title: What remains when the furniture goes?
items.description: WATCH exposes an outward-facing ring beside the long table. Returning to PAIR before VACANT lets the reader remove the furniture while keeping its rectangular rooms. These new comparisons precede the preserved proposal for future observations with people.
captions: WATCH: the seven-chair table beside eight backed seats and a raised centre; sixteen blocks in total.
VACANT: two unfurnished rectangular rooms. Walls, openings and scale remain authored.
items.image_note: 36 runtime checks, eight selected walking segments and 72 content checks pass. All six artifact families remain declared; five instantiate. The legacy tt and synthesis stand issues are recorded in the report. These two images show different plan states, not a controlled furniture-only pair.
items.text_kind: book — existing questions become selectable encounters
items.before: A future version could compare actual sightlines and turn-taking across the two plans. The ethical question would become a design question with observable consequences: which participant gained access, which difficulty remained, and what change should follow?
items.after:
WATCH puts another arrangement beside the long table: eight backed seats face outward around a raised centre. Follow one seat’s direction with your eyes. The ring has returned, but its invitation has changed. There is no watcher inside the model; the arrangement gives you a question to take to one.

Return to PAIR, then press VACANT. The furniture goes; the walls remain. An empty room still has sides, an opening and a scale. Removing the chairs has not removed every decision.

A future version could compare actual sightlines and turn-taking across the two plans. The ethical question would become a design question with observable consequences: which participant gained access, which difficulty remained, and what change should follow?

items.title: Do the branches actually meet?
items.description: JUNCTION leaves a gap. OVERLAP rotates both branches inward while their feet retain their positions. The visitor can remove the glowing marker to inspect what is there. The artifact moves nearer arrival; every supporting family stays.
captions: JUNCTION: separate uprights and a marker between them.
OVERLAP, marker hidden: two oriented boxes share a volume.
items.image_note: Actual states of the revised Godot museum from the same 1.7 m camera. The runtime check verifies a point inside both boxes in OVERLAP. This is geometry, not a logical inference test.
items.text_kind: book — an available comparison becomes an encounter
items.before: Trace branch A and branch B towards the lit junction. Inspect what remains visible on either side of that meeting point. Before deciding which branch should win, give each one a source and a reason to have arrived there.
items.after:
Trace branch A and branch B towards the lit junction. Look from the side. The light hangs between them, but do the branches actually meet? Press MARKER to take the glow away. Before deciding which branch should win, give each one a source and a reason to have arrived there.

Press OVERLAP. The feet keep their places while the branches lean inward and pass through one another. Walk around the crossing. Nothing has been cut to make room. The renderer lets both forms remain; deciding what their meeting means is still ahead of us.

items.title: Choose what you would keep. Then press RESOLVED.
items.description: The earlier source-only comparison is now selectable. A always keeps its height and takes the centre; B remains as a named stump. FORK restores both branches and separates their tops. The reader can disagree with the decision encoded in the sculpture.
captions: RESOLVED: A stands at full height; B is 0.2 m tall. No marker remains.
FORK: both heights return and the branches lean outward. The visible marker drops to their feet.
items.image_note: The source code example is unchanged. The artifact chooses these outcomes; it neither merges files nor derives consequences from contradictory propositions.
items.text_kind: book — an available comparison becomes an encounter
items.before: There is a second arrangement in the source that this placement does not show. In resolved, A keeps its full height and B becomes a labelled stump. The two builder calls make resolution visible as a change in what remains. That is an authored picture of a decision, not a proof that the decision was warranted.
items.after:
Before pressing RESOLVED, choose what you would keep. Then look down for B. A keeps its full height and takes the centre; B becomes a labelled stump. Did the decision agree with yours? The two builder calls make resolution visible as a change in what remains. That is an authored picture of a decision, not a proof that the decision was warranted.

Press FORK. Both branches regain their height and lean apart. If the marker is visible, it has dropped between their feet. Distance has changed; no new reason has been given for either account. Return to OVERLAP when you want to see what settlement shortened.

items.title: A name survives. What did it fail to record?
items.description: The closing return asks what must remain for a decision to be reconsidered. Marker visibility and viewpoint offer different ways to inspect the crossing; neither supplies the missing history of the accounts.
captions: OVERLAP with its authored highlight.
The same crossing from the side, with the highlight hidden.
items.image_note: 38 runtime checks, 24 selected walking segments and 73 content checks pass. The second image changes both camera and marker state. All eight families remain declared; seven instantiate. The vault floor is flush, but its broad footprint remains a placement follow-up. Headset verification remains open.
items.text_kind: book — an available comparison becomes an encounter
items.before: Return to the pillars and imagine a resolution that shortens one to a stump. What information should remain so the decision can later be reconsidered? Keeping a source, a date and the rejected alternative does not make revision automatic, but it prevents a settled display from hiding how settlement occurred.
items.after: Return to RESOLVED and find the small name beside B. A label remains, but it tells us little about what has been lost. What information should remain so the decision can later be reconsidered? Keeping a source, a date and the rejected alternative does not make revision automatic, but it prevents a settled display from hiding how settlement occurred.

items.title: One subject, four locations
items.description: The four existing panels face into the hall at full scale, with readable text and side controls. Begin with their original four-verdict comparison. Their map tokens assign the descriptions; visitor movement changes which panel can be read.
captions: NW: ORDERLY, 87%.
NE: CREATIVE, 64%.
items.image_note: Actual revised museum captures from equivalent local camera positions at two different stations. No classifier measures the visitor.
items.text_kind: book — following the claim to its source
items.before: Read the subject identifier on all four panels. Keep it fixed in your comparison, then note the verdict, the confidence and the footer on each. Look back at the first panel after reading the others: it has not become a different subject because another description is available.
items.after: Begin with FOOTNOTE on the four inward-facing panels. Read the subject identifier on each. Keep it fixed in your comparison, then note the verdict, the confidence and the small address below. Look back at the first panel after reading the others: it has not become a different subject because another description is available.

items.title: An appealing word also needs evidence
items.description: The mature passage stays. DANGEROUS is not made accountable by its high percentage; CREATIVE also needs criteria. All four station assignments and the shared subject remain intact.
captions: SW: DANGEROUS, 92%.
SE: IRRELEVANT, 22%.
items.image_note: This text is deliberately unchanged. These are different stations and authored values, not measured probabilities.
items.text_kind: book — following the claim to its source
items.before: Choose DANGEROUS and ask what evidence would make that judgement accountable. Dangerous to whom, under which circumstances, and according to what consequence? Then apply an equally precise question to CREATIVE. A favourable word also needs criteria; situatedness is not a licence to stop checking an appealing claim.
items.after: Choose DANGEROUS and ask what evidence would make that judgement accountable. Dangerous to whom, under which circumstances, and according to what consequence? Then apply an equally precise question to CREATIVE. A favourable word also needs criteria; situatedness is not a licence to stop checking an appealing claim.

items.title: Cover the address. What has the claim lost?
items.description: A source-only variant becomes a visitor action. COVER conceals the footer without changing the verdict, its percentage or its assigned subject. FOOTNOTE reverses that gesture.
captions: FOOTNOTE: the address is visible below the claim.
COVER: a strip hides the same address; DANGEROUS remains at 92%.
items.image_note: Same station and camera. Runtime checks confirm all four underlying text fields are identical; the change is physical occlusion.
items.text_kind: book — following the claim to its source
items.before: These are four authored readouts. Each panel retains the verdict assigned to it; your movement changes which panel you read. The percentages are supplied examples, not calibrated probabilities calculated from evidence about a real person. A high number in this room therefore cannot establish that its description is more trustworthy than a lower number.
items.after:
These are four authored readouts. Each panel retains the verdict assigned to it; your movement changes which panel you read. The percentages are supplied examples, not calibrated probabilities calculated from evidence about a real person. A high number in this room therefore cannot establish that its description is more trustworthy than a lower number.

Stay with DANGEROUS. Read its 92%, then press COVER. A strip lies across the address. The verdict and the number remain. Has the claim become easier to accept, or harder to ask about? Press FOOTNOTE to uncover the place it was speaking from. Nothing new has been learned about the subject.

items.title: Does a body make a claim more believable?
items.description: WITNESS exposes the existing marked base, height rule and symbolic eye. The new paragraph asks whether this frame changes trust. The earlier proposal for comparing real criteria and observations remains future work.
captions: FOOTNOTE: the claim on its simple stand.
WITNESS: a marked body and eye frame the unchanged claim.
items.image_note: Same camera. 63 runtime checks, ten selected walking segments and 84 content checks pass. Five authored placements remain. The creature was paused only for this private probe; headset and learner verification remain open.
items.text_kind: book — following the claim to its source
items.before: For the room’s next experiment, each panel could reveal a distinct criterion and the observation it used. A visitor could then compare disagreement caused by different evidence with disagreement caused by different definitions. The current four views supply the scaffold for that comparison.
items.after:
Now press WITNESS. The panel acquires a marked base, a height rule and an eye above it. Walk to its side. This eye has no sensor; it is part of the frame. Does giving the claim a visible body make you trust it more? Its 92% has still earned no additional evidence. Return to FOOTNOTE and take that suspicion to another panel.
